source_read: PMC HTML (saved text of PMC8098650, NIH author manuscript), read start to end: abstract (Importance, Observation, Conclusion and Relevance), Introduction, Biological Pathways/Neural Basis and Cognition, Clinical Presentation, Interventions with Table 1 as rendered text, Conclusion and Relevance, supplementary-material note, acknowledgements, financial disclosures and all 94 reference entries. Figures 1 and 2 are images absent from the text (legends only); the supplementary eTable is not in the save. The 'Author information' panel is collapsed, so affiliations could not be checked, and I had no way to see the published JAMA Psychiatry version or PubMed.

design.note: narrative-review is right. The ClinicalTrials.gov count is the only systematic element and has no stated search date or classification rules, so it does not make the paper a systematic review.

key_findings.note: Introduction ¶1. Recomputed (17,258 - 12,122)/12,122 = 42.4%, as printed. The NSDUH figures carry no numbered citation in the text; Figure 1 is an image, so the 195% could not be read off the figure.
Introduction ¶1; reference 3 is titled as a study of prescription stimulant trends 2006 to 2016, so the card's caveat holds.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed exactly as quoted, but it is in Clinical Presentation ¶2, not ¶3. That section has only three paragraphs (acute and psychiatric presentation; trajectories and course, including these figures; cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease). The 5-year remission figure of up to 30% without treatment is in the same paragraph.

key_findings.note: Clinical Presentation ¶1, all four figures, with the reference numbers as the card gives them.
Biological Pathways ¶3. The review adds that the extent of impairment is linked to older age, longer duration and higher frequency of use, also from that one study.

key_findings.correction: Content confirmed; the location is Clinical Presentation ¶3, not ¶4 (there is no ¶4). The sentence says methamphetamine 'is also present in 63% of opioid deaths', which the card's caveat to re-anchor in the MMWR report covers.

key_findings.note: Interventions ¶1 and Table 1. Recomputed from the table: 65/159 = 40.9%, 25/65 = 38.5%, 14/65 = 21.5%, 25/159 = 15.7%, 14/159 = 8.8%; the card's derived 11 unpublished (5 + 0 + 6) is correct and is labelled as the editors' inference in analysis.effect_sizes.

Interventions ¶1. One point worth keeping: the review's own sentence reads 'low-strength or insufficient evidence of no effect', which is self-contradictory; the card silently smooths it to 'low-strength or insufficient evidence on abstinence'. The smoothing is the right reading but the garble belongs with reporting issue 4.
Interventions ¶2. The review also gives an average retention of about 60 days alongside the 51% two-week dropout; the card omits that number, which is the more useful one for a claim about retention.
Biological Pathways ¶1 and the Figure 2 legend; the eight hypothesized neurotoxicity mechanisms and the Warburg passage are all in that paragraph, cited to references 10 to 22.
Conclusion and Relevance (penultimate point) and Biological Pathways ¶2 ('none of these measures have thus far been clinically useful').

reporting_issues.note: Abstract › Importance against Introduction ¶1. One addition: the only doubling in the text is of total stimulant use over the decade from the prescription-stimulant source, which may be where the abstract's 'doubled' came from; if so the abstract transfers a prescription-distribution trend to illicit use and mortality.

Confirmed independently from both sides: Paulus gives 'another 14%' for years 2 to 5, while my own reading of Brecht and Herbeck found 25% in that paper's abstract and 7 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 15% in its results. The 14% matches neither, so it is a third figure in circulation.

All four mismatches confirmed against the reference list: reference 50 is titled as a meta-analysis of substance-induced psychotic disorder; reference 81 covers cocaine and amphetamine addiction; reference 89 is about dropout in pharmacological treatment trials, not a treatment programme; reference 75 is titled a systematic review but is called a meta-analysis in the text.
Both confirmed in Interventions ¶1 (the registry address is spelled correctly later in the same paragraph). Add the self-contradictory 'insufficient evidence of no effect' from the same paragraph.

The author-manuscript title is confirmed from the saved text. The published title could not be checked: there is no browser in this session and the save contains no PubMed or publisher page. Reader 1's card says it was checked on PubMed; I can neither confirm nor contradict it.

risk_of_bias.note: Instrument and vocabulary are right: narrative-review with 'none-applicable' and the editors' checklist (METHODS §5.3), domain words from the low / some-concerns / high set, and overall 'high' equal to the worst domain. I reached the same five domain judgments independently. This is the one card of my five that applies the instrument the design calls for; sc_hemphill_2024 and sc_matsumoto_2014 use AMSTAR 2 for the same design and should be brought into line with this one.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Substantial' is right, and all six listed gaps check out: the abstract's doubling; the prescription-stimulant figure; 'results in significant long-term cognitive and neurological deficits' and 'possibly degenerative' against the body's own statement that the literature is debated and almost entirely cross-sectional; the Warburg passage resting on a cancer-biology reference; 'exercise helps to maintain abstinence' when the cited exercise studies measured craving, inhibitory control, depression and anxiety; and mirtazapine, which I confirmed appears nowhere in the text or reference list.

missed: The cardiovascular and cerebrovascular section (Clinical Presentation ¶3) has no key finding except the 63% opioid-death figure, although the card's can_establish offers the review as a pointer to that literature. Unrecorded statements from that paragraph: cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease as the most severe problems and leading cause of death; methamphetamine-related strokes rising, mostly in young men and primarily haemorrhagic; the associations with vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension, atherosclerosis, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy; the cardiomyopathy and electrocardiogram descriptions; and the symptoms preceding death attributed to methamphetamine toxicity. These are the statements most likely to be cited from this review and they need anchors with their reference numbers.

'Leading cause of death' is sourced to a 10-year cohort of cardiovascular and stroke risk (reference 66). A cohort estimating risk does not establish what people who use methamphetamine most often die of; this is the same kind of inference the card flags elsewhere and should be in the interpretation gap.

The stroke sentence ('primarily hemorrhagic in nature', reference 67) rests on the share of published cases in a case-report review, not on relative incidence. The same inference is in sc_hemphill_2024, and both cards should carry the caveat so that no monograph states it as a fact about incidence.

Clinical Presentation ¶2 presents a 'gateway' statement (adolescent cannabis use raising the probability of initiating methamphetamine, via biological and social processes, from one longitudinal study) and the trajectory claim that transition from casual to compulsive use takes about 50, 60 and 85 days from a single sample. Both are causal-sounding generalizations from single studies; the card holds the 50/60/85-day figures in the exposure field but neither is flagged in the interpretation gap.

The 42.4% rise in deaths is cited to a report titled as covering cocaine and psychostimulants with abuse potential, 2003 to 2017, while the text reads 'cocaine, amphetamines, or both' for 2015 to 2016; this belongs with the construct mismatches in reporting issue 3.
other_notes: Table 1's row label is the registry's 'Randomized Intervention Model', which the text reports as randomized clinical trials; the registry field and the design are not the same thing, so the 65 is an upper bound.
Figure 1 plots counts of published articles alongside past-year use, so it is partly a bibliometric figure; its values are not extractable from the text.

funding and declared_conflicts confirmed word for word from the Acknowledgements and Financial Disclosures; the manuscript lists disclosures for the first author only, as the card says. Affiliations (Laureate Institute for Brain Research; University of Tulsa) could not be checked in the save.

sample.selection_effects names references 29 to 31 and 33 to 37 as the authors' own: consistent with the reference list, where those entries carry Paulus or Stewart as an author (reference 32 does not).
